messages.author: c85836a0f56bb080
messages.subject: Outlier and model fitting
parts:
Hi Chris,

I am hoping to estimate the instantaneous speed/distance traveled by ground-dwelling shorebird chicks with ctmm. I tracked chicks from hatch using an automated radio telemetry network, and with the help of Chris Tyson, I was able to incorporate error ellipse for the trilateration estimates. I attached the outlier plots, variogram, and model selection results of one tag. I used an arbitrary 20m/s, 200m outlier filter, and it removed 40% of points. Should I try a more lenient filter? And it seems that the top-selected model overfits the variogram? Any insights on how I should approach this would be greatly appreciated, and please let me know if you need more context.

Thanks!
Feipeng

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Outlier and model fitting
parts:
Hi Feipeng,

Sorry for the delay. The 200-meter filter is definitely too strong, as it leaves you with a visible circle around the geometric median. The only distance outliers I could potentially see are the cluster of northern most points, but that could easily be a place that the bird actually visited, as there are several points there. Otherwise, I don't see a clear need for distance-based filtering.

With the larger speed point estimates, I'm curious as to how low their lower CI limit goes (is it plausible?). I also don't know what the biological speed limit is for this age/species. Visually, I don't see anything sticking out of the speeds, but you might turn the transparency up to see better. One issue I've seen with some radio telemetry networks is underestimated error ellipses, which results in an overall increase in speed estimates and decrease in autocorrelation timescale estimates. Are your chicks really moving ~25 km/day in short 10-15 second trips? Do you have any test/calibration data for the network?

With the variogram, I'd look if it keeps increasing in the second half (6-12 days) and if that corresponds to a weekly shift or expansion in their range.

best,
Chris

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Outlier and model fitting
parts:
Hi Feipeng,

There's a tradeoff between bias and precision, that you will need to consider if you don't have enough data in your time windows:
  1. speed() has a t argument to estimate over a range of times, while conditioning on all times in the data.
  2. The fit object used and whether or not it came from a larger set of data.
In both, you can condition on more data outside of your time window, to increase precision at the cost of bias. If the time windows are too short, then you can be forced to do this (DOF=0).

Both speed() and speeds() are continuous time and can handle gaps. They have different purposes.

Best,
Chris
